newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel denies plans to alter exchange rate policy.
newsitem.headline: Israel denies plans to alter exchange rate policy.

text.p: The Bank of Israel and the Treasury said on Tuesday that there are no plans to abolish the diagonal exchange rate or its trading band.
They were responding to a report in the newspaper Yedioth Ahronot this morning that central bank officials had proposed the measures in talks with the Finance Ministry.

"There has not been any proposal like this," the Bank of Israel spokesman told Reuters. "There are those in the Bank of Israel who support widening the band...but there was no talk about abolishing nor any operative decision."
In a statement the Treasury denied there were any plans and warned that the persistent rumours were causing damage.
"The unauthorised talk of abolishing the system only increases the downward pressure on the (currency basket) exchange rate and makes it more difficult to manage monetary policy," the ministry said.

The shekel is allowed to fluctuate in a trading band of seven percent above or below a sloping mid-point designed to devalue the Israeli currency at a rate of six percent a year against the basket of key currencies.

But in the last two weeks the basket rate has been scraping the bottom of the band, as the dollar strengthens in world markets against the other component currencies of the basket. As a result, the Bank of Israel has been forced to spend hundreds of millions of dollars supporting the basket.

In trading today, the basket representative rate was fixed at 3.6253 shekels compared with 3.6247 on Monday as the dollar continued to strengthen. The dollar was fixed at 3.3190 shekels versus 3.3068 on Monday.

A government source said he did not believe the bank was worried in the long run about the basket rate. "This is not the first time (the rate) has hit the bottom of the band...In the past it's corrected itself," he said.

The Bank of Israel announced on Monday it was lowering the base interest rate 0.5 percentage point this week to 14.2 percent, but analysts said the reduction would not be enough to influence the foreign exchange market. They said high domestic interest rates had been a major factor over the last two years in the shekel's strength.

Government sources said the Treasury was opposed to widening the band out of fear it would cause an appreciation of the shekel against the dollar. The Treasury would have to approve any change in the band or diagonal rate.

The Bank of Israel spokesman said a package of foreign currency liberalisation measures had been completed and had been awaiting Treasury approval for some time. He said the measures would ease foreign currency restrictions for companies and financial institutions but denied today's reports in Yedioth that they included changes in exchange rate policy.
